note: Original structured classroom practice. Independent academic review pending.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Relate energy to doing work in an everyday setting.
questions.prompt: A porter raises a crate from the ground onto a loading platform. Explain what energy allows the porter to do and identify where the porter gets the energy used by their muscles.
questions.answer: Energy allows the porter to do work by lifting the crate against gravity. The muscles use energy made available from food.
questions.explanation: Raising the crate increases its gravitational potential energy. The porter transfers energy to the crate while lifting it.

markingGuide.description: Connects energy to doing work on the crate.
Identifies food as the source for the muscles.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Identify energy stored by changing an object's shape.
questions.prompt: A foam cushion is held compressed under a board. Name the form of energy stored because of the compression and predict what the cushion will do when the board is lifted away.
questions.answer: The compressed cushion stores elastic potential energy. It expands towards its earlier shape when the load is removed.
questions.explanation: Deforming an elastic object stores energy that can cause movement as its shape recovers.

markingGuide.description: Names elastic potential energy.
Predicts expansion towards the original shape.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish energy due to height from energy due to motion.
questions.prompt: A marble is held still at the top of a ramp. Later it rolls near the bottom. Identify the energy it has because of its height at the start and the energy it has because it is rolling later.
questions.answer: At the top it has gravitational potential energy relative to the bottom. While rolling it has kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: The two observations refer to different properties of the marble: its position and its motion.

markingGuide.description: Identifies gravitational potential energy.
Identifies kinetic energy.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain energy transformation using evidence from a device.
questions.prompt: A pupil says that a buzzer creates energy when connected to a cell because the room was quiet before. Correct the pupil's explanation and use the sound as evidence of an energy transformation.
questions.answer: The buzzer receives energy electrically and transforms part of it into sound energy as its vibrating part moves. The sound shows that energy has appeared in a different form.
questions.explanation: The silence before connection says nothing about the energy available from the cell. The buzzer needs energy supplied through the circuit.

markingGuide.description: Identifies that energy is supplied electrically rather than created.
Connects vibration or sound with output in another form.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Trace useful energy changes through a generator and lamp.
questions.prompt: A torch has a hand crank, a small generator and a lamp. It lights while the handle is being turned. Give the energy change at the generator and then the change that gives the user light.
questions.answer: The generator converts mechanical energy from the turning handle to electrical energy. The lamp converts some of the electrical energy to light.
questions.explanation: The generator and lamp carry out different steps in the energy pathway.

markingGuide.description: Gives mechanical to electrical at the generator.
Gives electrical to light at the lamp.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the usefulness of an energy output depends on the intended task.
questions.prompt: A fan motor makes a loud hum while moving air. A door alarm makes a similar hum while warning a shopkeeper. Explain why the sound output is useful in one device and may be unwanted in the other.
questions.answer: The alarm's sound alerts the shopkeeper. The fan is intended to move air, so its hum can be a distraction and is an output that does not directly cool the user.
questions.explanation: The same form of output can be desired in one device and incidental in another.

markingGuide.description: Explains the sound's intended role in the alarm.
Identifies airflow as the purpose of the fan and explains why its noise may be unwanted.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Connect an energy transformation to a practical use.
questions.prompt: A tailor uses an electric iron to smooth a creased cotton uniform. Identify the energy transformation in the heating element and explain how its output helps the tailor.
questions.answer: The element transforms electrical energy into thermal energy. The hot soleplate transfers energy to the cloth while it is pressed, helping to relax the creases.
questions.explanation: The useful result combines heat with pressure on the fabric.

markingGuide.description: Identifies electrical to thermal energy.
Explains how heating helps smooth the fabric during pressing.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain renewable and non-renewable sources using their replenishment times.
questions.prompt: A community uses sunlight to dry cassava slices and natural gas to heat water. Explain why these sources fall into different groups even if cloudy days interrupt cassava drying.
questions.answer: Sunlight is renewable because it is continually supplied on human timescales despite changes in availability. Natural gas is non-renewable because deposits form far more slowly than people use them.
questions.explanation: Renewability refers to replenishment. Availability at a given time depends on local conditions.

markingGuide.description: Classifies sunlight and connects it to replenishment on a human timescale.
Classifies natural gas and compares formation with use.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Classify wind and coal by their underlying energy sources.
questions.prompt: A wall map marks a station whose turbines turn in moving air and another that burns coal to make steam. Identify the source in each case and group it as renewable or non-renewable.
questions.answer: Moving air, or wind, is a renewable source. Coal is a non-renewable fuel.
questions.explanation: Both stations may produce electricity through rotating machinery, while the original sources differ.

markingGuide.description: Identifies wind as renewable.
Identifies coal as non-renewable.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Describe a use of renewable energy that does not involve generating electricity.
questions.prompt: A hostel has a solar collector through which water passes on its way to an insulated tank. Explain how sunlight helps provide warm water and why the tank is insulated.
questions.answer: The collector absorbs energy from sunlight and transfers thermal energy to the water. Insulation reduces the rate at which the stored water loses heat.
questions.explanation: Solar energy can heat water directly. The tank helps retain that heat until the water is needed.

markingGuide.description: Explains transfer of energy from sunlight to the water through the collector.
Explains the purpose of the insulation.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain how overusing a potentially renewable resource can reduce its supply and affect land.
questions.prompt: A village gets fuelwood from a woodlot. Each year more trees are cut than grow to replace them. Predict what happens to its fuelwood supply over several years and explain one consequence of losing ground cover.
questions.answer: The supply of harvestable trees declines. Where less vegetation covers the ground, rain can wash away more exposed soil.
questions.explanation: Renewable resources can be depleted locally when use exceeds recovery.

markingGuide.description: Predicts declining supply and links it to harvesting faster than replacement.
Explains a plausible effect of reduced ground cover.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Explain how reliable energy for refrigeration can improve a community service.
questions.prompt: A farmers' cooperative starts operating a reliably powered cold room for vegetables that it will sell the next day. Describe how the energy service can affect both the produce and the sellers.
questions.answer: Refrigeration slows spoilage in suitable produce. Keeping more of it saleable may reduce sellers' losses and allow more vegetables to reach buyers.
questions.explanation: The outcome depends on maintaining appropriate storage conditions for the produce.

markingGuide.description: Connects refrigeration with slower spoilage.
Gives a reasoned benefit for the sellers or their customers.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.learningObjective: Demonstrate how two sources can supply a common service through different pathways.
questions.prompt: Draw two labelled arrow diagrams for lighting a classroom. In one, sunlight reaches a photovoltaic panel that powers a lamp during the day. In the other, diesel runs a generator that powers a lamp. Show the route to the light and label the source in each diagram as renewable or non-renewable.
questions.answer: Sunlight (renewable) → photovoltaic panel → electrical energy → lamp → light. Diesel (non-renewable) → engine and generator → electrical energy → lamp → light.
questions.explanation: Both pathways supply electrical energy to the lamp. In the diesel system the engine first provides mechanical energy to turn the generator.

markingGuide.description: Shows the solar route through the panel and electricity to light.
Shows the diesel route through the generator and electricity to light.
Correctly labels both source categories.

questions.subject: Intermediate Science
questions.subtopic: Solar power for a health service
questions.learningObjective: Explain an application of renewable energy and storage in healthcare technology.
questions.prompt: A clinic uses solar panels and a charged battery to power a refrigerator that stores vaccines. Explain the jobs of the panel and battery and why maintaining the required storage temperature matters.
questions.answer: The panel produces electrical energy from sunlight. The battery stores energy chemically and can later supply electricity to the refrigerator. Keeping the required temperature helps preserve the vaccines' effectiveness.
questions.explanation: The panel and battery support the refrigerator at different times. The refrigerator uses electricity to remove heat from the storage compartment.

markingGuide.description: Explains how the panel supplies electrical energy.
Explains how the battery provides electricity later.
Links suitable storage temperature to protecting vaccine effectiveness.
